_readme: Quick-round authoring, v2 (v1 pairs/ladders retired 2026-07-12 — owner verdict: not fun). Two games. combination: the daily vault word — 5-letter acquisition terms, one per Zulu day (date-seeded index, same word for every visitor); each carries a one-line definition ('def') and a cite resolved to Described-in chips. governs: Which Part Governs — one-line situations ('s'), the governing part label ('p'), three hand-set adjacent-plausible distractor part labels ('d'); 'cite' resolves the review link. Part names live in 'part_names' for the button subtitles. Figures/rules must trace to the deck/corpus — a wrong game answer is a credibility incident, not a bug.

combination.def: The boundary of the bargain — modifications live inside it or become new procurements.
A written demand for payment as a matter of right — certified over $100K, and the clocks start running.
Acceptance of an offer — the moment the Government is bound.
A response the Government can accept to form a binding contract — quotes aren't one.
What analysis must prove fair and reasonable — on every single action.
The examination of contractor records that backs up cost analysis on the big ones.
Performance and payment protection — required on construction over $150,000.
Information, not an offer — the Government's order is the offer; the vendor can still walk.
Excusable or not — the fork that decides whether a default termination survives.
No money, no contract — obligation without appropriation is an Antideficiency Act problem.
Giving up a known right — like the HCA waiving certified cost or pricing data.
The clauses that allocate risk — read them before the contractor does.
Allowable, allocable, and reasonable — a cost must clear all three to be paid.
The contracting officer's final decision — the document that starts every appeal clock.
Best value — the basis of every source selection, tradeoff or lowest-price-technically-acceptable.
Who owns the property — it passes by the clause, not by who paid.
The Board of Contract Appeals — 90 days from the final decision, or 12 months to the COFC.
Only a warranted agent binds the United States — apparent authority binds nothing.
A task or delivery order — fair opportunity governs who gets it.
Exclusion from Government contracting — check SAM before every award.
Trade agreements open foreign sources above their thresholds — Buy American below.
Small-business participation targets — the subcontracting plan carries them past $900K.
Procurement integrity's hard edge — report it, never negotiate around it.
Describe the need, not the vendor — restrictive specifications kill competition.
Service and construction labor standards — wage determinations ride the contract.
Labor-hour and T&M contracting — the ceiling and surveillance are the safeguards.
Firm-fixed-price — one price, whatever it costs; the contractor owns the risk.
Assistance, not acquisition — if the purpose is public benefit, it isn't a contract at all.
Limitation of Cost and Funds — the ~75% notice that keeps cost-type work funded.
Economic price adjustment rides a published index — protection, not speculation.
The share ratio — how incentive contracts split every dollar of overrun and underrun.
'Brand name or equal' — the salient characteristics define what equal means.
The cure notice gives 10 days to fix a failure — skip it only for pure late delivery.
A novation moves the contract when companies do — the Government must recognize the successor.
The GPC holder's lane — micro-purchases to $15K, spread fairly, never split.
DPAS-rated orders jump the queue — DO and DX ratings are mandatory to accept.
Data rights follow the money — who funded development decides what the Government may do.
Multiyear and options stretch a contract — about five is the services rail.
The bona fide need — this year's money buys this year's requirement.
The CICA stay — file at GAO within 10 days of award or 5 of debrief, and performance stops.
Think before you buy — the written strategy that lines up requirement, market, and schedule before a dollar moves.
Rent or buy? The lease-versus-purchase analysis you run before committing the government to owning something.
Float it before you fix it — the pre-solicitation version you circulate so industry can sharpen the requirement.
The legal reason you're competing less than fully — one of the named exceptions, each carrying its own justification.
How evaluation turns judgment into a rating — adjectival, color, or number, but always tied to the factors you published.
The short list after the first cut — the offerors still realistically in the running, the ones you hold discussions with.
One determination covering a whole category of actions, so you don't re-justify the same thing buy after buy.
You're buying the effort, not a deliverable — a set level of labor aimed at a broadly stated task.
Who bears the cost of the unknown — fixed-price puts it on the contractor, cost-reimbursement on the government.
The split that decides how much of an overrun or underrun each side eats — the heart of an incentive arrangement.
Labor and indirect rates — the multipliers that turn hours into a bill, and exactly what DCAA shows up to audit.
The paperwork endgame — final invoice paid, property disposed, releases signed, file closed.
Money the contractor owes back — overpayments, unliquidated advances, financing the government will collect.
Where the protest goes — the agency, GAO, or the Court of Federal Claims, each with its own forum and clock.
The Court of Federal Claims — where a contractor can take a claim instead of, or after, the board of contract appeals.
The one holding the contract with the government — every subcontractor below flows their work up through them.
What you can't accept from someone doing business with the government — the line between a courtesy and a bribe.
The quiet sibling of fraud and abuse — not criminal, just money spent with nothing to show for it.
Sealed bidding — price only, no negotiation: bids come in sealed, open in public, and the low responsive bidder wins.
Changed the requirement mid-solicitation? Amend it — in writing, to every offeror, before proposals are due.
Best value is about worth, not just price — what the government actually gets for the money, tradeoffs and all.
How R&D gets picked — scientific and technical merit through a Broad Agency Announcement, not lowest price.
A binding contract needs a contracting officer with actual authority — without it you have an unauthorized commitment, not a deal.
Wages the government makes you pay — Service Contract Labor Standards set the floor for the people doing the work.
You can't lien federal property, so payment bonds stand in — the surety pays the subs and suppliers a prime stiffs.
Splitting one requirement into smaller buys to duck a threshold or competition — a classic prohibited move.
'Brand name or equal' — when only a specific product will do, and the written justification that unlocks it.
The third of fraud-waste-abuse — authority or resources bent to the wrong ends, even when no crime is charged.

governs.s: Your customer insists only one vendor can possibly do the work.
An offeror protests your award decision to the GAO.
The contractor submits a certified written demand for $180K over Government-caused delays.
The program manager wants to add a new test requirement mid-performance.
The mission changed — the Government no longer needs the last 40 units.
Performance is strong and the base year ends in 60 days.
Market research just found exactly two capable small businesses.
A $180K commercial buy the office needs fast.
The item sells in the commercial marketplace with only minor modifications.
Before drafting anything, you need to know who out there can actually perform.
A $30M requirement needs its documented strategy before you solicit.
Competitive proposals are in — exchanges, competitive range, discussions.
Choosing between firm-fixed-price and cost-plus for a risky development effort.
Check AbilityOne and Federal Prison Industries before the open market.
Your apparent awardee was indicted for fraud last week.
A vendor rep offers your technical evaluator playoff tickets.
The contractor requests progress payments on a long production run.
Is the contractor's holiday party an allowable cost?
The contractor will use Government-owned test equipment for the effort.
A $2M construction award — what protects the subs and guarantees completion?
Buying design and construction of a new maintenance hangar.
Writing a services PWS with measurable performance outcomes.
Wage determinations for the janitorial services contract.
The lowest quote is on foreign-made end items.
Funding university research through a broad agency announcement.
Describing the requirement without naming the incumbent's product.
Where the upcoming solicitation must be announced, and for how long.
You and the lawyer disagree about what 'commercial product' means.
Who may sign for the Government — and within what dollar limits.
Where the signed contract file lives, and what must be in it.
Which clause goes in the contract — and whether you may tailor it.
The unit needs work started tonight — the price gets negotiated later.
The deliverable software arrived with restrictive markings on every file.
An unauthorized commitment just landed on your desk for ratification.
Two responsible sources exist but the J&A cites 'unusual and compelling urgency.'
The 8(a) firm wants the follow-on sole source at $28M (DoD).
Your GPC holder wants to split a $28K buy across two months.
An offeror demands to know why they lost — within three days of notice.
The awardee's SAM registration lapsed between proposal and award.
Consolidating five base services contracts into one — small businesses object.
The contractor claims constructive changes from the COR's 'suggestions.'
Exercising the option, but the price now looks 15% above market.
A commercial item termination — cause, not default.
The IGCE says $95M — certified cost or pricing data or an exception?
The incumbent wrote the requirements document for the follow-on.
The contractor stopped paying its subs — they're calling you.
Adding 90 days to the schedule after a hurricane — no cost change.
Ordering off another agency's IDIQ — what document and what fee?
The requirement is inherently governmental — can a contractor do it at all?
A quote came in under the IGCE by 40% — award it?
The awardee wants to swap in a different (cheaper) subcontractor.
Buying laptops — accessibility standards apply to the acquisition.
The security deposit question: performance bond or letter of credit?
Sealed bids, public opening, award to the low responsive bidder.
The contractor's cost proposal buries unallowable lobbying costs.
Terminating for convenience — what does the settlement include?
A HUBZone firm claims the price evaluation preference in full and open.
The Government furnished the tooling late — the contractor wants money.
Defining 'day,' 'shall,' and 'may' for the whole rulebook.
Synopsizing the award itself — when is that required?
An IDIQ holder complains the last three orders skipped fair opportunity.
The prime wants Government property title transferred at contract end.
Progress payments vs. performance-based payments — which is preferred?
The A-E firm must be selected on qualifications, not price.
A first-tier sub on the hangar job never got paid — payment bond claim.
Setting the NAICS code and size standard for the solicitation.
The contractor invoked the Excusable Delays clause after a supplier fire.
Undefinitized work hit 50% of the not-to-exceed — what stops?
The small business was found non-responsible — SBA gets a shot.
Locking the option price at award vs. negotiating it at exercise.
Publicizing a J&A after award — the transparency requirement.
The data was developed entirely at private expense — what may the Government do?
